description: We are ATLAS, an engineering team from Mexico developing modular monitoring technologies using sensors, electronics, and data visualization. Our interests include space exploration, extreme environments, and intelligent systems. We aim to use NASA's open data to develop practical solutions. We welcome collaborators with skills in programming, data analysis, hardware, and space science.
summary:
ATLAS Analog Explorer is a bilingual (English/Spanish) geospatial decision-support platform designed to discover and evaluate Earth's most suitable analog locations for future human missions to Mars.

Using NASA POWER and Martian reference data, ATLAS analyzes over 17,000 geographic cells across the Americas, comparing solar radiation, temperature, thermal variation, atmospheric dust, elevation, and terrain slope.

Users can select Martian regions, customize environmental variables and their weights, and explore ranked locations through interactive maps, satellite imagery, topographic layers, and 3D globes.

Beyond environmental similarity, ATLAS evaluates three critical research objectives: life-support systems, controlled food production, and water recycling. It also incorporates crew health risks, accessibility, transportation logistics, construction materials, and adjustable cost estimates.

Each candidate location includes comparative environmental indicators, suitability scores, operational considerations, and downloadable technical reports. The platform explicitly identifies conditions that cannot be replicated on Earth.

ATLAS transforms open scientific data into an accessible mission-planning tool. Future development aims to expand its geographic coverage worldwide, incorporate additional mission types, and support increasingly complex exploration scenarios, contributing to safer, more sustainable human exploration of Mars and beyond.
details:
ATLAS Analog Explorer — Project Details

Project Overview

ATLAS Analog Explorer is a bilingual (English/Spanish) geospatial decision-support platform developed to identify and evaluate terrestrial locations that could serve as analog research environments for future missions to Mars.

Our project was developed around a central question: What makes a location on Earth not only environmentally similar to Mars, but also suitable, accessible, safe, and economically feasible for conducting research?

Rather than focusing exclusively on geographical resemblance, ATLAS integrates environmental science, engineering, logistics, economic considerations, and human health into a unified evaluation system.

How Does ATLAS Work?

The current prototype analyzes more than 17,000 geographic cells across the Americas, using NASA POWER environmental data and Martian reference conditions.

Users can select reference regions on Mars, including Jezero Crater, Gale Crater, and Elysium Planitia, and customize the environmental characteristics they wish to compare.

The platform evaluates variables such as solar radiation, average temperature, thermal variation, atmospheric dust, elevation, and terrain slope. Users can activate or deactivate variables, modify their relative importance, and apply geographic filters.

ATLAS then generates a ranking of potential analog locations, which can be explored through interactive maps, satellite imagery, topographic layers, and 3D globes.

Each selected location includes environmental comparisons, suitability indicators, logistical information, human-health considerations, and downloadable PDF technical reports.

The platform currently supports three experimental research objectives:

  • Life-support and environmental control: evaluating environments for testing habitat stability, thermal management, and protection systems.
  • Controlled food production: exploring conditions relevant to greenhouse technologies and sustainable food production.
  • Water recycling and recovery: identifying environments for testing water treatment, reuse, and resource-management technologies.

What Makes Our Project Creative?

The creativity of ATLAS lies in approaching planetary analog research as a multidisciplinary decision-making challenge rather than a simple geographical search.

A location might resemble Mars environmentally but be unsuitable for establishing a research base because of transportation difficulties, high costs, limited infrastructure, or potential risks to the crew.

ATLAS addresses this challenge by evaluating three complementary dimensions:

Environmental and scientific similarity: How closely does a terrestrial location resemble selected Martian environmental conditions?

Logistical and economic feasibility: How accessible is the location? How far is it from roads, cities, airports, or ports? What materials might be needed, and what are their estimated costs?

Human health and safety: What risks could the location present to a research crew? How might altitude, temperature, dust, solar exposure, or distance from medical assistance affect operations?

By combining these dimensions into a customizable evaluation system, ATLAS helps users compare not only where experiments could take place, but also which locations may be more practical for different research objectives.

The platform includes adjustable scoring criteria, preliminary construction-material estimates, transportation considerations, and crew-health indicators.

It also identifies important limitations of terrestrial analog environments, recognizing that conditions such as Martian gravity, atmospheric pressure, and ionizing radiation cannot be fully reproduced in an open-air location on Earth.

This transparent approach helps prevent environmental similarity from being confused with complete physical equivalence.

Technologies, Programming Languages, and Resources

ATLAS was developed using Python and TypeScript, with Visual Studio Code as the primary development environment.

The team used laptops for programming, data processing, platform development, testing, and visualization.

The project incorporates publicly available scientific resources from NASA, particularly NASA POWER environmental information and Martian reference data, to support comparisons between terrestrial and planetary conditions.

The platform combines geographic datasets, configurable evaluation algorithms, interactive visualization, and downloadable technical documentation.

Its bilingual interface makes the information more accessible to Spanish- and English-speaking users.

The current implementation is software-based and does not require specialized hardware to operate.

Factors Considered During Development

Our team deliberately avoided focusing only on technological capabilities.

We considered how a potential analog research location would function as part of a complete operational system, where environmental conditions, engineering requirements, economic resources, infrastructure, and human well-being influence one another.

For example, a scientifically promising location may present significant challenges if construction materials are difficult to transport, nearby infrastructure is limited, or emergency medical assistance is far away.

For this reason, ATLAS incorporates preliminary accessibility assessments, transportation and material-cost estimates, and crew-health risk indicators.

The platform also allows users to adjust the importance of different evaluation criteria according to their research priorities.

We believe that effective mission planning requires considering not only whether a technology can operate under challenging conditions, but also the resources, infrastructure, and people needed to make that operation possible.

Benefits and Expected Impact

ATLAS aims to support researchers, engineers, students, and organizations involved in planetary exploration and terrestrial analog research.

By integrating multiple evaluation criteria into one platform, ATLAS can help users identify promising research locations, compare alternatives, understand operational constraints, and make more informed preliminary planning decisions.

Its potential benefits include reducing the time required for initial site screening, improving visibility into logistical and economic challenges, and encouraging the consideration of crew safety from the earliest planning stages.

The platform could support research involving environmental-control systems, sustainable food production, water recovery, habitat materials, and other technologies relevant to long-duration space exploration.

Future Vision

Although the current prototype focuses on the Americas and experimental research bases for Mars, ATLAS was conceived as an expandable platform.

Our future goals include extending geographic coverage worldwide, incorporating additional mission types such as robotic exploration and surface operations, and expanding the environmental, technical, economic, and human factors considered during evaluation.

We also envision incorporating more detailed infrastructure information, operational constraints, resource availability, and mission-specific requirements to support increasingly comprehensive planning scenarios.

In the longer term, the platform could be adapted to evaluate terrestrial analog environments for other planetary destinations.

Our vision is to transform ATLAS into a comprehensive, accessible, and adaptable decision-support tool that connects scientific exploration with engineering feasibility, economic responsibility, and human safety.

Explore Earth. Prepare for Space.
